examples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{2}-3t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(2t+1)\underset{\sim}{j}$. Find its position when $t=4$.
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=10\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+10\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$. Find its exact position when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
A particle starts at $(-2,4)$. After $t$ seconds it has moved $3t$ units right and $t^{2}$ units down from its starting point. Write its position vector function for $t\ge0$.
A particle moves in a straight line at a steady rate. It is at $(5,8)$ when $t=2$ seconds and at $(17,0)$ when $t=6$ seconds. Find its position vector function.
examples.solution_text:
The coordinate changes occur over $6-2=4$ seconds.

$\begin{aligned}\text{Horizontal change per second}&=\frac{17-5}{4}=3\\\text{Vertical change per second}&=\frac{0-8}{4}=-2\end{aligned}$

Track back two seconds to find the initial position.

$\begin{aligned}x(0)&=5-3(2)=-1\\y(0)&=8-(-2)(2)=12\\\underset{\sim}{r}(t)&=(3t-1)\underset{\sim}{i}+(12-2t)\underset{\sim}{j}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(2t+1)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t+9)\underset{\sim}{j}$, with coordinates measured in metres. Find its distance from the origin when $t=2$ seconds.

A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{2}-25)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^{2}-3t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge0$.

(a) Find its position when it crosses the $y$-axis.

(b) Find all times when it is on the $x$-axis.
examples.solution_text:
(a) On the $y$-axis, $x(t)=0$.

$\begin{aligned}t^{2}-25&=0\\t&=5\end{aligned}$

The negative root is excluded by $t\ge0$.

$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{r}(5)&=(25-25)\underset{\sim}{i}+(25-15)\underset{\sim}{j}\\&=10\underset{\sim}{j}\end{aligned}$

(b) On the $x$-axis, $y(t)=0$.

$\begin{aligned}t^{2}-3t&=0\\t(t-3)&=0\end{aligned}$

So $t=0$ or $t=3$.

examples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{2}-t-12)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^{2}-16)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge0$. Show that it passes through the origin and find when this occurs.
examples.solution_text:
At the origin, both components must be zero at the same time.

$\begin{aligned}t^{2}-t-12&=0\\(t-4)(t+3)&=0\end{aligned}$

For $t\ge0$, the only candidate is $t=4$. Check the other component:

$\begin{aligned}y(4)&=4^{2}-16\\&=0\end{aligned}$

Both components are zero at $t=4$, so the particle passes through the origin then.

examples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(1+t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(4-t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge0$, where $t$ is measured in seconds. Describe its motion.

A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t-7)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t+1)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge0$, with coordinates measured in metres and $t$ in seconds. Find when it is closest to the origin and its exact distance then.
examples.solution_text:
Minimise the squared distance, which has its minimum at the same time as the distance.

$\begin{aligned}\left|\underset{\sim}{r}(t)\right|^{2}&=(t-7)^{2}+(t+1)^{2}\\&=2t^{2}-12t+50\end{aligned}$

This quadratic opens upwards. Its minimum occurs at

$\begin{aligned}t&=-\frac{-12}{2(2)}\\&=3\text{ s}\end{aligned}$

This time satisfies $t\ge0$.

$\begin{aligned}\left|\underset{\sim}{r}(3)\right|&=\sqrt{(3-7)^{2}+(3+1)^{2}}\\&=\sqrt{32}\\&=4\sqrt{2}\text{ m}\end{aligned}$

examples.derivation: At t=4, x=16-12=4 and y=8+1=9. The position is 4i+9j.
cos(pi/6)=sqrt(3)/2 and sin(pi/6)=1/2, giving the exact position 5sqrt(3)i+5j.
Add the horizontal displacement 3t to -2 and subtract the downward displacement t² from 4. Thus r(t)=(3t-2)i+(4-t²)j for t≥0.
The elapsed time is 4 seconds; coordinate rates are 12/4=3 and -8/4=-2. Tracking back from t=2 gives (-1,12), so r(t)=(3t-1)i+(12-2t)j. Substitution at t=2 and t=6 recovers both given positions.
At t=2 the position is (5,11). Its distance from the origin is sqrt(25+121)=sqrt(146) metres.
For the y-axis, t²-25=0 gives t=±5; only t=5 is admissible, when y=25-15=10. For the x-axis, t²-3t=t(t-3)=0 gives both admissible times t=0 and t=3.
The horizontal component factors as (t-4)(t+3). Its only non-negative zero is t=4, and the vertical component then equals 16-16=0. Hence the particle passes through the origin at t=4.

The initial position is (1,4), and each second changes the coordinates by (1,-1). The path is x+y=5 with x≥1. The diagram's marked points (1,4) and (2,3), and its arrow towards increasing x and decreasing y, agree with this motion.
The squared distance is (t-7)²+(t+1)²=2t²-12t+50=2(t-3)²+32. Its minimum on t≥0 occurs at t=3 seconds. The position is (-4,4), giving distance sqrt(32)=4sqrt(2) metres.
